transcript:
Meeting header:
- Date/Time: 2026-10-29 15:00 UTC
- Duration: 58 minutes (recorded)
- Attendees: Samira (Redwood AE), Diego (Redwood SE), Lena (Redwood SE), Mark (AcumenHead ML Infra), Priya (SRE), Omar (ML Eng), Jill (Security)

Summary:
Short technical deep dive to triage nondeterministic kernel selection and CUDA-graph replay failures that coincide with quantized paths and KV cache warmstart on AcumenHealth's private VPC cluster. Goal is to establish telemetry capture steps, triage hypothesis (quantization+priming cause path divergence), and agree next steps: traces, quant sweep, and benchmark rerun.

Topics: kernel selection behavior, CUDA graph replay/"replay healing" heuristics, KV cache priming vs steady state, quantization precision shifts, NVTX / Nsight capture, on-prem VPC constraints and upload process, fallback policies.

Transcript:
[00:00] Samira: hey everyone thanks for carving the time, um this is Samira from Redwood. we wanted to focus on the repeatable repro you mentioned on the ticket, the nvgraph replay failures and kernel path flips when quantized.
[00:12] Mark: yeah thanks, we started seeing more of it when we rolled quantized 4-bit profiles on a subset of our services. cold starts are fine but after a few requests the CUDA graph replay will sometimes error out or recompile and then latency spikes.
[00:26] Diego: when you say "replay error out" can you paste the exact log? is it a cudagraph replay mismatch or a launch timeout?
[00:34] Priya: most often we see a segfault in the Cuda graph replay path, sometimes it recovers and replays a new graph, other times the process aborts and we fallback to a lower tier. logs give mixed signals, stack shows mismatch in the kernel arg buffer.
[00:48] Lena: ok, and this only shows up on the quantized model variants? or also FP16?
[00:54] Omar: 90% on quant 4-bit, occasionally on 8-bit there's a related path but much rarer. FP16 looks stable. we suspect the kernel selection matrix changes with quantized kernels and then the cudaGraph capture used at warmstart picks a different kernel set than replay expects.
[01:12] Diego: that matches a hypothesis we've seen: quantization changes tensor layout or kernel launch parameters, nsync of the KV cache priming can cause kernel path divergence between capture and replay. we call the mitigation 'replay healing' where we detect mismatch and either re-capture or patch the replay path.
[01:31] Jill: from security we also need to confirm what traces are collected and where they get uploaded. our cluster is private — VPC peering only — so we need a secure upload flow.
[01:40] Samira: absolutely. we'll provide an upload presigned S3 link to your restricted bucket with client-side encryption, and a checklist of what to redact.
[01:48] Mark: great. what telemetry should we capture? nvtx? nsight? pprof?
[01:53] Diego: nvtx markers plus a short Nsight system trace (5-10 seconds around the failure) is the most useful. also capture the CUDA graph capture record, if possible serialize the graph object and the model config + tokenizer state. the tricky bit is KV priming state — capture the sequence of prompt tokens that lead to warmstart.
[02:12] Omar: we can do that. one note — on our on-prem nodes we have limited disk for Nsight traces, we might need to stream them directly to the upload link, or run a trimmed trace.
[02:23] Lena: trimmed traces still help; focus on the capture and replay window. please include the model binary SHA, quant params (scale/zero point), and any custom kernel flags.
[02:34] Mark: okay good. the other pattern is that eviction/hot-swap from another tenant on the same host occurs right before the replay failure — do you think noisy neighbor could cause kernel selection instability?
[02:44] Diego: noisy neighbor can change GPU clock states or memory bank affinities which can alter kernel heuristics. if the runtime uses heuristics that consider SM occupancy or available scratch memory, that can flip to a different kernel variant. combined with quantization -> different kernel, capture/replay mismatch becomes possible.
[03:02] Priya: so is the fix to make capture/replay more conservative, or to change the kernel heuristics?
[03:07] Diego: both are valid. short-term we often pin kernel variants for deterministic replay when quantized models are used. medium-term we improve 'replay healing' logic to detect kernel id mismatch and attempt a controlled re-capture; long-term we update kernel selection to be more stable under small resource changes.
[03:28] Samira: can you walk us through the reproduction we have? Mark, you shared a perf log and a small prompt set.
[03:34] Mark: yes, it's in the ticket. sequence: 1) cold launch with kv priming prompts (few short dialogues), 2) scale to 4 concurrent streams, 3) after ~30s one pod shows cudaGraph replay abort, latency jump from 35ms to 450ms, then fallback.
[03:48] Diego: sounds like warmstart into steady state then eviction. do you use persistent KV cache between requests or per-session?
[03:55] Omar: persistent per-container persistent KV cache, we prime on container start with a set of representative prompts to avoid token-by-token warmup cost.
[04:05] Lena: that priming changes the cache shape and length distributions, so the sequence length distribution for capture differs from subsequent replays — important to capture that.
[04:15] Samira: two quick triage hypotheses: (A) quantized kernel selection results in different kernel IDs between capture and replay because of layout/launch param changes; (B) eviction/noise changes device state causing heuristic flip; (C) serialization/deserialization of CUDA graph misses a pointer or buffer alignment on certain quant types. any other thoughts?
[04:34] Mark: sounds right. also we saw one log pointing at mixed-allocator fallback in the runtime during replay.
[04:40] Diego: mixed-allocator interactions with quantized kernels can change alignment. that's a good callout.
[04:45] Priya: if we pin kernel variant, does that increase tail latency?
[04:49] Diego: pinning can slightly increase average latency if the pinned kernel isn't optimal for all sequence lengths, but it buys determinism. Redwood has runtime policies to pin only for the capture/replay window or under specific quantization profiles.
[05:05] Omar: what's the overhead of enabling replay healing?
[05:08] Lena: healing adds a short detection window: on mismatch, we either re-capture once (cost included) or switch to safe fallback (slower kernel) and queue a re-capture during low load. overhead is typically 2-3% in token throughput for those few seconds.
[05:21] Samira: let's get into the telemetry steps so Diego can start bisecting offline.
[05:25] Diego: step 1: run with nvtx markers around capture and replay. include a short Nsight trace capturing the graph capture, replay, and the moment of abort. step 2: dump the serialized cudaGraph and the kernel IDs list. step 3: capture the quant params file plus tokenizer state and the exact prompt sequence used for priming. step 4: if possible capture memory allocator stats and GPU clock/power state.
[05:48] Omar: we can do 1-3, 4 might be limited but we'll try.
[05:53] Diego: also capture gdb backtrace on crash if possible. but that may require debug symbols.
[05:58] Jill: security: we need Redwood's data handling policy in writing before we upload traces.
[06:03] Samira: we'll attach the policy and the upload presigned link. traces will be limited TTL and only our infra team will access.
[06:09] Mark: good. any quick mitigations we can try now?
[06:13] Diego: try running quantization with per-tensor symmetric scaling turned off — sometimes scale distribution differences change kernel offsets less. also experiment with disabling aggressive kernel heuristics via runtime flag --kernel-heuristic-level=stable.
[06:27] Omar: ok we'll flip those flags and run bench.
[06:30] Priya: if we do pinned kernels, how do we monitor for regressions?
[06:33] Lena: Redwood Console will report per-model token latency percentiles and also surface kernel-level telemetry under the Per-Route->Kernel tab. we'll set an anomaly alert for >2x p99.
[06:45] Samira: quick note on on-prem upload: since you have VPC restrictions, we will provide a small sftp agent that can run in your cluster and securely upload the traces to our intake for analysis. the agent is lightweight, signs manifests, and can be audited.
[06:58] Jill: we need that agent's source and a short threat model.
[07:02] Samira: sure, will provide.
[07:05] Diego: for the bisect, I'll be looking for differences in kernel ID sequences between capture and replay. if we can get the serialized kernel list that's ideal. we'll also run a targeted microbenchmark locally that reproduces the same tensor shapes and quant params to see if we can trigger path flip.
[07:23] Mark: how often do you see this resolved by re-capture vs changing kernels?
[07:27] Diego: about 60% resolved with a single re-capture, 30% by pinning, remainder required deeper kernel/allocator changes.
[07:34] Omar: any tooling to automatically detect when capture is non-deterministic?
[07:38] Lena: yes, Redwood runtime emits a "capture checksum" and on replay we compare; mismatch increments a metric. we can turn on verbose capture-checkmode to log telemetry without recovering, helpful for debugging.
[07:53] Priya: let's talk about quantization fuzzing — how granular should our sweep be?
[07:58] Diego: start coarse: 8-bit -> 6-bit -> 4-bit with per-tensor vs per-channel scaling. log kernel selection at each. if you see divergence at 4-bit per-tensor, try per-channel. record accuracy delta too.
[08:12] Mark: we worry about end-user quality too, not just perf. will Redwood help automate the sweep?
[08:17] Samira: yes, Redwood Optimize can run a batch sweep and produce a report showing latency, kernel-path variance, and quality regression. we can run it against your eval set once you share.
[08:27] Omar: good. timeline — we'll capture and upload traces by EOD Friday, run the coarse quant sweep by Monday and upload. Can Diego triage mid next week?
[08:36] Diego: yes, I'll bisect and prepare a short findings doc.
[08:40] Samira: any other topics?
[08:42] Jill: compliance around trace retention — what's the TTL?
[08:45] Samira: default retention 30 days for debug traces; we can shorten/extend per contract.
[08:51] Mark: one more edge case: multi-GPU graphs where NVLINK causes a different kernel split. is that something you can check?
[08:59] Diego: absolutely, include topology info and peer-to-peer bandwidth logs. kernel planner sometimes chooses fused kernels if NVLINK available; if NVLINK toggles it can flip planner decisions. include the PCI bus topology dump.
[09:14] Omar: will do.
[09:16] Samira: recap/outcomes: 1) Redwood to share upload link, agent, and security policy (Samira) 2) Customer to collect nvtx + Nsight around failure, serialized cudaGraph and quant params + prompt set (Omar/Mark) 3) Diego will bisect kernel id sequence and run local microbench (Diego) 4) follow-up triage in one week.
[09:40] Diego: small technical note: when serializing cudaGraph ensure the pointer offsets are normalized; we have a script for that — I'll include it.
[09:49] Mark: thanks.
[09:51] Priya: thanks everyone.
[09:53] Samira: thanks all, we'll send the artifacts and a calendar invite for the follow-up.
